topics.title: Chapter 1 — Introduction to Administrative Law (pp. 1–15)
topics.description: Classes 1–2: agency structure and functions; administrative law sources; federal/state APAs; models of agency legitimacy. Includes the p. 15 problem, retained without an answer.

entries.title: Administrative agency
entries.summary: A unit of government other than the chief executive, legislature, or courts, with statutory authority to affect rights or duties of persons outside government.
entries.laymanExplanation: An agency is a government body empowered by law to make decisions affecting people or businesses.
entries.legalExplanation: Agencies are institutional units exercising delegated statutory powers, typically within the executive branch but sometimes independent. Their names, leadership, and institutional structures vary.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 1
entries.examApplication: Identify the agency, the statutory delegation, and the agency action before analyzing procedures or review.

entries.title: Agency leadership, structure, and jurisdiction
entries.summary: Agencies can be led by one or several officials and may be called departments, commissions, or boards; size, caseload, and specialization vary.
entries.laymanExplanation: Not all agencies look the same; some handle millions of decisions and others very few.
entries.legalExplanation: Heads generally are appointed by the chief executive, although some state officers are elected or appointed by legislatures. Agencies can address economy-wide subjects or sector-specific regulation.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 1–2

entries.title: Core administrative powers
entries.summary: Agencies may investigate, prosecute, make rules, adjudicate, license, set rates, administer benefits, and perform other delegated functions.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agencies can make detailed rules, investigate violations, decide individual cases, and give benefits or licenses.
entries.legalExplanation: An agency may exercise several governmental functions within one institution, creating both efficiency and procedural-fairness concerns.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 2, 7–11
entries.examApplication: Classify the action as rulemaking, adjudication, licensing, enforcement, or another function; identify the governing procedures.

entries.title: Regulatory versus beneficiary agencies
entries.summary: Regulatory agencies control conduct and enforce legal obligations; beneficiary agencies distribute benefits, loans, or grants.
entries.laymanExplanation: Some agencies police regulated conduct; others administer government assistance.
entries.legalExplanation: The distinction is functional rather than a rigid structural category. Examples in the text include immigration, securities and environmental regulation versus Social Security and veterans' benefits.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 2

entries.title: Administrative law versus substantive regulatory law
entries.summary: Administrative law governs common legal principles of agencies, including procedures, allocation of authority, and judicial review; substantive regulatory law governs the programs those agencies enforce.
entries.laymanExplanation: Administrative law is about how an agency exercises power, not necessarily the detailed policy it enforces.
entries.legalExplanation: The field cuts across agency subject matters similarly to civil procedure and evidence; it concerns rulemaking and adjudication processes and checks by courts, legislatures, and chief executives.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 2
entries.examTrap: Do not confuse a substantive immigration, tax, or environmental issue with an administrative procedure or review issue.

entries.title: Why lawyers study administrative law
entries.summary: Federal, state, and local agencies affect benefits, taxes, licenses, immigration, banking, land use, environmental matters, businesses, and other legal practices.
entries.laymanExplanation: Nearly every area of legal practice involves government agency decisions.
entries.legalExplanation: Representing clients before agencies requires knowledge of the applicable substantive scheme alongside administrative procedures and review mechanisms.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 2–3

entries.title: Administrative law and changing political priorities
entries.summary: The text describes changing deregulatory and regulatory priorities across the Trump and Biden administrations and recent judicial constraints on agencies.
entries.laymanExplanation: The balance between government regulation and deregulation changes with politics and court decisions.
entries.legalExplanation: The book expressly states its perspective was written after the 2024 election but before the January 2025 inauguration; its forward-looking predictions are historical commentary, not a statement of later outcomes.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 3
entries.examTrap: Treat the casebook's statements about anticipated future developments as publication-era context.

entries.title: Regulation — broad meaning
entries.summary: In the broad sense, regulation means government policy affecting markets, including policies created by statute.
entries.laymanExplanation: A statute controlling a market is regulation in the broad sense.
entries.legalExplanation: Broad-sense regulation can result from legislative enactments, and repeal of such a statute is broad-sense deregulation.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 3

entries.title: Regulation — narrow meaning
entries.summary: In the narrow sense, a regulation or rule is an agency's generally applicable, legally binding pronouncement implementing a statute.
entries.laymanExplanation: A rule is a binding agency instruction for the public, such as banning a specified pollutant discharge.
entries.legalExplanation: A rule issued under delegated authority may establish rights and duties of regulated persons; repeal of an agency rule is deregulation in the narrow sense.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 3
entries.examTrap: Distinguish general agency rules from guidance documents, which the chapter describes as nonbinding.

entries.title: State, local, and federal administrative law compared
entries.summary: The text deliberately examines state and local administrative law alongside federal law because these systems differ and local practice is common.
entries.laymanExplanation: Federal APA rules do not automatically describe what a state or city agency must do.
entries.legalExplanation: Differences among jurisdictions provide comparison points; attorneys must consult the appropriate jurisdiction's enabling acts, procedures, and precedents.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 3–4
entries.examApplication: Ask whether the actor is a federal, state, or local agency before applying a particular APA.

entries.title: Sources of administrative law
entries.summary: Sources include constitutions, statutes (especially APAs), and judge-made common law.
entries.laymanExplanation: Agency procedure comes from constitutional rules, legislation, and court decisions.
entries.legalExplanation: The applicable legal framework depends on the jurisdiction and the agency-specific statutory scheme.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 4

entries.title: Administrative Procedure Acts (APAs)
entries.summary: The federal government and every state have APAs; they are general and comprehensive procedural statutes addressing agency rulemaking, adjudication, information access, and review.
entries.laymanExplanation: An APA is a broad rulebook for how agencies operate and how their decisions can be challenged.
entries.legalExplanation: Federal and state APAs govern many agencies but can differ materially; general statutes coexist with agency-specific enabling legislation.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 4
entries.examApplication: Identify whether the relevant APA provision covers the agency and type of action.

entries.title: Federal APA of 1946 and its political compromise
entries.summary: The federal APA was enacted in 1946 after political struggles concerning New Deal agencies; it balanced procedural constraints on agency power with agency flexibility.
entries.laymanExplanation: Congress allowed powerful agencies but required processes and review designed to protect people affected.
entries.legalExplanation: The text quotes George B. Shepherd's account criticizing the idea that enactment represented unqualified consensus; it emerged as a hard-fought political compromise.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 4–5

entries.title: Model State Administrative Procedure Acts
entries.summary: The 1961 MSAPA influenced more than half the states; the 1981 model was more ambitious but little adopted; a 2010 model was less elaborate and had limited adoption according to the text.
entries.laymanExplanation: States share some procedural models, but there is no single uniform state APA.
entries.legalExplanation: State APAs generally govern state rather than local agencies; model acts are templates, not themselves automatically binding law.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 5–6
entries.examTrap: Do not treat any MSAPA as governing a state unless it has been enacted there.

entries.title: Administrative Conference of the United States (ACUS)
entries.summary: ACUS generates reports and recommendations aimed at improving federal administrative processes.
entries.laymanExplanation: ACUS studies how agency procedures can work better.
entries.legalExplanation: The text describes ACUS as a federal advisory body using staff, academic consultants and volunteers; it was defunded in 1995 and resumed in 2009.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 6

entries.title: Automobile Insurance Commission (AIC) hypothetical
entries.summary: A state creates an Automobile Insurance Commission under a general statute banning unfair and discriminatory insurance practices to illustrate the agency process.
entries.laymanExplanation: A vague law needs an agency to turn general goals into specific actions.
entries.legalExplanation: The hypothetical shows how the agency receives legislative authority and funding, develops policy, regulates individual parties, and faces multiple oversight mechanisms.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 6–11
entries.examApplication: Use AIC as the recurring fact pattern for identifying administrative functions and controls.

entries.title: Research and publicity
entries.summary: Agencies can gather information, commission studies, publish findings, and provide information that helps markets and the public.
entries.laymanExplanation: An agency may inform the public without forcing anyone to follow a new rule.
entries.legalExplanation: The AIC hypothetical includes comparisons of premiums, consumer complaints, and educational FAQs as informational tools.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 6

entries.title: Rulemaking — general binding policy
entries.summary: Rulemaking translates broad statutory directives into generally applicable binding rules; the text describes notice, public comment, agency consideration, and publication.
entries.laymanExplanation: The agency fills in details for everyone, not just one named person.
entries.legalExplanation: APA rulemaking procedures may require advance notice, participation, explanation, and publication. Valid rules must be consistent with delegated statutory authority.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 6–7
entries.examApplication: Ask whether the rule is legally binding, generally applicable, procedurally proper, and within statutory authority.
entries.examTrap: The chapter emphasizes stronger procedural transparency and statutory scrutiny for agency rules than for statutes.

entries.title: Guidance documents (nonbinding agency statements)
entries.summary: Agencies issue guidance under names such as interpretive rules, manuals, bulletins, rulings, and policy statements; this chapter describes such federal guidance as nonbinding and generally issuable without formal procedures.
entries.laymanExplanation: Guidance says what an agency thinks or plans; it ordinarily cannot command conduct as a binding legislative rule.
entries.legalExplanation: Terminology and procedures differ across jurisdictions; the excerpt states some states subject guidance to procedures required for binding rules.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 7–8
entries.examTrap: A document's title alone does not decide whether it is a binding legislative rule.

entries.title: Licensing
entries.summary: A license authorizes a person or entity to engage in specified conduct; an agency may set qualifications and sanctions including revocation.
entries.laymanExplanation: You may need agency permission before working in a regulated profession or activity.
entries.legalExplanation: Licensing systems promote quality or safety but can create barriers to entry, higher prices, and opportunities for industry capture.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 8
entries.examApplication: Look for statutory licensing authority, qualification standards, and procedures for denying or revoking the license.

entries.title: Regulatory capture and barriers to entry
entries.summary: A regulated industry may influence the agency so that regulation protects incumbents instead of the public; licensing can restrict entry unnecessarily.
entries.laymanExplanation: Rules meant to protect consumers can instead protect existing businesses from competition.
entries.legalExplanation: The text treats capture and unnecessary licensing burdens as costs that must be weighed against benefits.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 8

entries.title: Permits
entries.summary: A permit is a type of license requiring agency permission before a specified action.
entries.laymanExplanation: You must obtain approval before starting certain activities.
entries.legalExplanation: Permit systems can be justified for dangerous activities but can impose administrative cost and delay.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 8

entries.title: Clearance system
entries.summary: A regulated party gives advance notice and may proceed if the agency does not affirmatively stop the action.
entries.laymanExplanation: Notify the government first; if it doesn't object, proceed.
entries.legalExplanation: A clearance mechanism is less intrusive than mandatory preapproval and shifts responsibility to the agency to intervene.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 8

entries.title: Investigation and enforcement
entries.summary: Agencies may collect reports, investigate complaints, subpoena records, inspect premises, and pursue enforcement through administrative or judicial proceedings where authorized.
entries.laymanExplanation: An agency must detect rule violations and take action; rules do not enforce themselves.
entries.legalExplanation: Investigation and prosecution are functions of delegated authority; agencies may initiate an internal administrative complaint or seek relief in court.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 8–9

entries.title: Adjudication — particular application
entries.summary: Adjudication determines legal rights or obligations of specified persons, unlike generally applicable rulemaking.
entries.laymanExplanation: A rule applies broadly; adjudication resolves a particular person's dispute or case.
entries.legalExplanation: Adjudication can address license revocations, benefits, enforcement proceedings, or certain private-party disputes delegated to agencies.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 9
entries.examApplication: Classify the action by whether it determines a specific party's legal rights or imposes generally applicable policy.

entries.title: Administrative adjudication and procedural fairness
entries.summary: State and federal APAs and constitutional due process may require impartial adjudicators and fair procedures, often including trial-type evidentiary hearings.
entries.laymanExplanation: An agency deciding your individual case may have to give you a fair chance to be heard.
entries.legalExplanation: An administrative judge may preside and the result can often be appealed internally to agency leadership; the precise hearing entitlement depends on applicable law.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 9

entries.title: Differences between courts and agency adjudication
entries.summary: Agency judges may play a more active role, usually without juries; specialized agencies often combine rulemaking, investigation, prosecution, and adjudication.
entries.laymanExplanation: An agency tribunal is court-like but is not the same as an ordinary court.
entries.legalExplanation: The chapter emphasizes specialized expertise and multiple functions in agencies, unlike the generalist and purely adjudicatory role of ordinary courts.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 9–10

entries.title: Ratemaking
entries.summary: Agencies may be delegated authority to set prices or rates, often when market failures or natural monopolies justify intervention.
entries.laymanExplanation: Government sometimes decides what a regulated company may charge.
entries.legalExplanation: Ratemaking may look like rulemaking for industry-wide rates or adjudication for company-specific rates and typically requires extensive economic analysis.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 10
entries.examApplication: Determine whether the rate order is industry-wide or specific and what procedural model is appropriate.

entries.title: Judicial review of agency action
entries.summary: Courts generally review final rules and adjudications for legal error, procedural error, factual support, constitutionality, or arbitrary exercise of discretion.
entries.laymanExplanation: A court can examine whether an agency acted lawfully and reasonably.
entries.legalExplanation: Access to review, timing, standard of review, and the proper division of authority between agency and court are recurring doctrinal questions.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 10
entries.examApplication: Identify finality, the available court, grounds of challenge, and applicable review standard.

entries.title: Freedom of information
entries.summary: Federal and state FOIA statutes require publication of certain agency materials and permit public requests for records subject to exceptions and judicial enforcement.
entries.laymanExplanation: People can ask agencies to release government records.
entries.legalExplanation: Information-access statutes promote transparency but impose administrative costs; exclusions and jurisdictional rules apply.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 10

entries.title: Legislative and executive oversight
entries.summary: Legislatures monitor, investigate, change enabling statutes, and use budgets; executives appoint and supervise agency leadership and may exercise removal authority.
entries.laymanExplanation: Congress or state lawmakers and governors or the President can influence agencies in different ways.
entries.legalExplanation: The exact powers vary by jurisdiction and agency independence; the excerpt discusses appointment, removal, budgets, investigations, and possible legislative controls over rules.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 11

entries.title: Agency-specific sources must also be consulted
entries.summary: A client matter may require the enabling statute, agency-specific substantive and procedural rules, and relevant administrative and judicial precedents.
entries.laymanExplanation: General admin law is only the starting point; check the rules of the actual agency.
entries.legalExplanation: The casebook emphasizes diversity of agencies and practical knowledge of how an agency operates.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 11

entries.title: Agency legitimacy
entries.summary: Administrative agency power should be lawful, fair, accurate, reasonably economical, and accepted as politically legitimate.
entries.laymanExplanation: People must have reasons to accept decisions by powerful officials who usually weren't elected.
entries.legalExplanation: Legitimacy theories attempt to justify delegated lawmaking and adjudicatory power in constitutional government.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 11

entries.title: Transmission-belt theory
entries.summary: Agency legitimacy derives from carrying out policy choices already made by elected legislatures; agencies must remain within statutory bounds and follow fair procedure.
entries.laymanExplanation: The legislature decides policy; the agency carries out instructions.
entries.legalExplanation: The text criticizes the model because many enabling statutes delegate broad discretionary decisions rather than resolving major questions.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 11–12
entries.examApplication: Consider whether an agency's broad policy discretion undermines the idea that it merely executes legislative choices.

entries.title: Expertise model of legitimacy
entries.summary: New Deal-era theory justified broad delegations because specialized expert agencies could solve complex economic and social problems.
entries.laymanExplanation: Experts are trusted to make technical decisions legislators cannot manage.
entries.legalExplanation: The theory favors broad agency authority and insulation from unwarranted political or judicial intrusion, but expert judgments also entail political tradeoffs.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 12

entries.title: Pluralist / interest-representation model
entries.summary: Agency action is legitimate when affected interests are fairly represented in an agency's political decision process.
entries.laymanExplanation: Let affected groups participate, then weigh their competing views.
entries.legalExplanation: The model emphasizes access and representation but risks resource disparities, capture, and inadequate attention to the public interest.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 12

entries.title: Civic-republican / deliberative model
entries.summary: Agency legitimacy comes from reasoned public deliberation that seeks the common good, not merely bargains among interest groups.
entries.laymanExplanation: Everyone gets a voice, and the agency explains its reasoning rather than just counting political influence.
entries.legalExplanation: The model favors notice-and-comment, transparent meetings, information access, and reasoned explanation; criticism emphasizes procedural delay and possible ossification.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 12–13

entries.title: Procedural-regularity theory
entries.summary: Agency lawmaking gains legitimacy from procedurally regular participation, especially APA notice and comment.
entries.laymanExplanation: Fair, open steps make agency decisions more acceptable.
entries.legalExplanation: Procedure enables public participation and creates a record that may support later judicial review.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 13

entries.title: Checks-and-balances theory
entries.summary: Agency power is restrained through judicial, legislative, and executive oversight.
entries.laymanExplanation: No agency has the last word on every question; other branches can check it.
entries.legalExplanation: Judicial review, legislative oversight and appropriations, and executive appointment and supervision offer overlapping controls, although monitoring is costly and imperfect.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 13

entries.title: Fire-alarm theory of administrative procedure
entries.summary: APA notice and comment alerts interested groups to agency changes so they may intervene through comments or enlist legislative or executive assistance.
entries.laymanExplanation: Public notice acts like an alarm so affected groups can react before a rule is final.
entries.legalExplanation: The excerpt connects procedural regularity with political oversight and attributes the fire-alarm model to public choice theory.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 13

entries.title: Libertarian critique of the administrative state
entries.summary: Some theorists regard extensive federal agency regulation and adjudication as incompatible with separation of powers and individual liberty.
entries.laymanExplanation: Some critics think agencies have too much power and regulation interferes excessively with freedom and markets.
entries.legalExplanation: The excerpt describes Philip Hamburger's constitutional critique and Adrian Vermeule's rebuttal, presenting this as a contested normative debate rather than settled law.
entries.source: Asimow & Levin, State and Federal Administrative Law (6th ed. 2025), Chapter 1, p. 13–14

problems.title: § 1.7 — Cannabis Control Board problem
problems.prompt: A voter initiative legalizes recreational marijuana but does not establish a regulatory agency or detailed standards. As Commerce Committee staff, prepare a memo discussing whether the state legislature should establish a Cannabis Control Board (CCB), what the legislation should provide, and which subjects the CCB's regulations should cover. Consider the alternatives of local government or existing criminal/tort law and the possibility of agency research, rulemaking, licensing, enforcement, and adjudication.
